newsitem.title: USA: Democrats seek to cut fund-raising investigation.
newsitem.headline: Democrats seek to cut fund-raising investigation.

text.p: House Democrats Wednesday vowed to block a Republican plan to spend millions of dollars probing White House fund raising, as the top Republican investigator was accused of pressuring foreigners for donations.

A former lobbyist for Pakistan accused Indiana Republican Representative Dan Burton, chair of the House committee investigating possible White House fund-raising abuses, of shaking him down for donations, according to the Washington Post.
Republican leaders dismissed the charges but Democrats used them to escalate complaints Burton was running a heavy- handed, partisan investigation.

Democrats promised to use parliamentary tactics to block his funding request, which they said would provide up to $20 million for the probe. They called on Republicans to expand the investigation to cover possible congressional fund-raising problems.

"Dan Burton has abused his power and the Republican leadership has been willing to allow him to run over the rules of the House in this investigation," said House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, a Missouri Democrat.
Democrats sent a letter to House Speaker Newt Gingrich vowing to fight any funding bill unless changes were made.

The Washington Post reported that Burton had sought campaign funds last year from a former lobbyist for Pakistan. When the lobbyist, Mark Siegel, said he could not raise the money, Burton allegedly threatened to cut off the lobbyist from contacts with Burton's congressional colleagues.

Burton was not available for comment and cancelled a meeting of his House Government Reform and Oversight Committee that had been scheduled for Wednesday. That committee is conducting the House probe of improper or illegal campaign funds for the 1996 election.
A Senate committee and Justice Department task force also are investigating questionable foreign and other funds given to Democrats that might violate U.S. campaign laws.
New Jersey Democratic Representative Frank Pallone, speaking on the House floor, said Burton should recuse himself from the investigation because of the allegations against him.
"It is this kind of hypocrisy that makes the American public so jaded about our American campaign financing system," said Pallone.
Separately, assistant House Republican leader Tom Delay of Texas dismissed criticism of Burton.
DeLay told reporters Burton was "one of the most upstanding members of Congress that I know."
"To have a Democratic lobbyist make those charges, just consider the source," DeLay commented in reference to Siegel, a former Democratic Party official.

Siegel, who had been a lobbyist for the government of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, said he was approached by Burton early last year to raise "at least $5,000" for his re-election campaign, the Post reported.

When he was unable to do so, Siegel said, the congressman complained to the ambassador for the Bhutto government at the time in Washington and later threatened to make sure "none of his friends or colleagues" would meet with Siegel or his associates.

"I should tell you," Siegel wrote July 25 in a two-page memo to a Bhutto aide in Islamabad, "that I worked in Washington for over 25 years and have never been shaken down by anyone before like Dan Burton's threats."
The Post said the memo was made available to the newspaper by a Democratic source in Congress and that Siegel confirmed its authenticity in an interview Tuesday.

"No one has ever dared to threaten me into contributing money, and no one has ever followed through on such threats by contacting one of my clients," Siegel wrote. "Despite what you may see in the movies, this isn't the way most U.S. politicians conduct themselves."
Burton, besides running the House fund-raising probe, is a longtime member of the House International Relations Committee and co-chairs an informal caucus on U.S.-Pakistani relations.
